newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Network Ten float details undecided - Asper.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Network Ten float details undecided - Asper.

text.p: Canadian businessman Israel Asper said on Wednesday he had not thought about how much of Australian television network Ten Group Ltd he would like to retain after it was floated.
"I haven't reflected on it," Asper told reporters.
But he said his CanWest Global Communications Corp was already discussing details of the float with Australian financial institutions.
"A float can take many forms and really the financial community will decide what is achieveable," Asper said.
"We welcome the concept of a serious group of Australian shareholders coming into Network Ten who have a shared vision of where the company can go," he said.

Asper's CanWest recently increased his economic stake in the Ten Group to 76 percent from 66 percent, although his voting interest remained in line with foreign investment ownership limits of 15 percent.

Asper was in Canberra to discuss the level of control he has over the television network with Communications Minister Richard Alston. Earlier in the week, he gave evidence to the Australian Broadcasting Authority on the same issue.

"We made a very full and frank disclosure as to what not only had happened, but what we expected and hoped and intended would happen in the future," Asper said of his discussions with Alston. "I believe he is now fully briefed and so is his staff."

He said he was in Australia for the long-term unlike fellow Canadian Conrad Black, who sold out of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd on Monday because of frustrations with the foreign ownership limits.
"We are here forever. We want to be part of the Australian media scene for a long, long time unlike some people who get beleaguered," he said.
He also said he would welcome any liberalisation of the foreign ownership rules.
"We are here to try and persuade Australians that there is great advantage to Australia in opening its arms and its doors to foreign investment in a much broader way," he said.
"But whatever the law is, we'll respect it."
A statement from Alston said it was inappropriate for the government to comment on the discussions until the ABA had finished its investigation into the control of Ten.
Asper will appear before the ABA again on Thursday.
